title: Collecting every coupon
objectives: Solve the coupon collector problem with linearity.

screens.title: Both faces of a coin
screens.prose: Flip a fair coin until you have seen both a head and a tail. The chain shows how many faces you have seen.

state.caption: Faces seen so far. Each arrow carries the chance of a flip moving you along it.

screens.question: How many flips do you expect to make?

hints.text: What does the first flip always give you?
After one flip, each flip is new with chance $\tfrac12$.
A chance of $\tfrac12$ per flip takes 2 flips on average: $1 + 2 = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the wait at the first flip.

byKey.two: You allowed one flip per face. After the first flip, the next repeats it half the time.
byKey.four: You waited 2 flips for each face. The first flip is always new, so it takes exactly 1.

explain.text: The first flip always shows a new face. After it, each flip shows the other face with chance $\tfrac12$, which takes 2 flips on average. In all, $1 + 2 = 3$.

screens.title: A new face
screens.prose: Now roll a fair die. With $k$ faces seen, a roll shows a new face with chance $(6 - k)/6$. A wait for something of chance $p$ per try is a **geometric wait**: it takes $1/p$ tries on average.

state.caption: Faces of the die seen so far, 0 to 6. Arrows carry the chance of each roll.

screens.question: You have seen one face. How many more rolls do you expect until a new one?

hints.text: What is the chance a roll is new?
Five of six faces are new.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The chance of a new face is $\tfrac56$; the wait is its reciprocal.

byKey.chance: That is the chance one roll is new. The wait is its reciprocal, $\tfrac65$.
byKey.five: You counted the unseen faces. Turn them into a chance first: $\tfrac56$ per roll.

explain.text: Five of the six faces are new, so each roll succeeds with chance $\tfrac56$. A geometric wait with chance $p$ averages $1/p$ tries: $\tfrac65 = 1.2$ rolls.

screens.title: Three different faces
screens.prose: Keep rolling the die. Each stage is its own geometric wait.

state.caption: Faces of the die seen so far, 0 to 6. Arrows carry the chance of each roll.

screens.question: How many rolls do you expect until you have seen three different faces?

hints.text: Three stages: 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3 faces.
Their chances are $1$, $\tfrac56$ and $\tfrac46$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the expected waits of the first three stages.

byKey.one-each: You allowed one roll per new face. Repeats cost extra rolls in stages 2 and 3.
byKey.no-first: You left out the first roll. It always shows a new face, and it still counts.

explain.text: The stages wait 1, $\tfrac65$ and $\tfrac64$ rolls. **Linearity** adds expected values whatever the dependence, so the total is $1 + 1.2 + 1.5 = 3.7$.

screens.title: Every face
screens.prose: Now wait for all six faces. Fill in the last three stages and the total.

state.caption: Faces of the die seen so far, 0 to 6. Arrows carry the chance of each roll.

screens.question: Fill the gaps.

hints.text: Each expected wait is $1/p$.
With three faces seen, $p = \tfrac36$, so the wait is 2.

feedback.correct: Waits of 2, 3 and 6, and a total of $14.7$ rolls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each wait is 1 over its chance; the total adds all six.

byKey.r5c2: With five faces seen, only one face is new: the wait is $1/\tfrac16 = 6$.

explain.text: The waits are $6/6, 6/5, \dots, 6/1$. Their sum is $6(1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac16) = 14.7$. Half of it, 6 rolls, is the last face alone.

screens.title: The slow half
screens.prose: Split the die wait in two: the first three new faces, then the last three.

state.caption: Each arrow now carries the expected rolls for that stage.

screens.question: Once three faces are seen, how many more rolls do you expect until all six?

hints.text: Which stages remain?
Three, two and one faces are new in turn.

feedback.correct: $2 + 3 + 6 = 11$ rolls, three times the first half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the waits of stages 4, 5 and 6.

byKey.mirror: That is the first half. The last three faces are rarer to find, so they take longer.
byKey.half: You split 14.7 evenly. The stages are not equal: late ones are slow.

explain.text: The first three faces take 3.7 rolls and the last three take 11. As a check, $3.7 + 11 = 14.7$. Most of a coupon wait is spent hunting the last few types.

screens.title: About six?
screens.prose: Asked how many rolls it takes to see every face, one candidate says "about 6, one per face". Another says "$6 \times 6 = 36$". The chart shows the exact chances.

params.xLabel: Rolls to see all six faces

state.caption: Exact chances of finishing on each roll, from the stage chain.

screens.question: What is the expected number of rolls?

options.why: You allowed one roll per face. Six rolls show every face only $6!/6^6 \approx 1.5\%$ of the time.
You gave every face the last face's wait of 6. Only the last takes 6 rolls on average; the first takes 1.
You waited $k$ rolls for the $k$-th face. The $k$-th new face takes $6/(7 - k)$ rolls.

hints.text: The stages are not equal.
The first stage takes 1 roll and the last takes 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the six stage waits.

byKey.b: Six rolls are the fewest possible, not the average. The bar at 6 is about 1.5%.

explain.text: Six rolls is the minimum, reached with chance $720/46656 \approx 1.5\%$. The waits run from 1 roll to 6, and they add to 14.7. The most likely count is 11, but the long right tail pulls the mean up.

screens.title: Stages add
screens.prose: Every wait here split into stages, each a geometric wait, added by linearity. With $n$ equally likely types, stage $k$ succeeds with chance $\tfrac{n - k + 1}{n}$, so $$E[T] = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{n}{n - k + 1} = n\left(1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1n\right) = nH_n.$$ This is the **coupon collector** problem.
screens.question: With $n$ types, which stage takes longest on average?

options.why: The first try always finds a new type, so the first stage takes exactly 1.

options.text: All stages take the same time
options.why: Each stage has fewer new types left, so its chance falls and its wait grows.

feedback.correct: The last stage has chance $\tfrac1n$ per try, so it waits $n$ tries.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the chances at the first and the last stage.

explain.text: Stage $k$ waits $n/(n - k + 1)$ tries, from 1 at the start to $n$ at the end. $H_n$ grows like $\ln n$, so the total grows like $n \ln n$.

screens.title: The argument
screens.prose: Put the coupon collector argument together, one justified line at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Split the wait: $T = T_1 + \dots + T_n$, with $T_k$ the wait for the $k$-th new type.
In stage $k$, $k - 1$ types are seen, so a try is new with chance $p_k = \tfrac{n - k + 1}{n}$.
A geometric wait with chance $p_k$ averages $E[T_k] = 1/p_k = \tfrac{n}{n - k + 1}$.
Multiply the stage waits, because every stage must happen.

hints.text: What do you write $T$ as?
Start with the split into stages.
Split, chance per stage, mean per stage, then add.

feedback.correct: Split, find each chance, average each wait, add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the wait into stages first, then take expectations.

byKey.d1: Stages happen one after another, so their times add. Multiplying is for chances of events that must all happen.
byKey.left-out: All four true lines belong in the argument.
byKey.s4: Linearity adds the stage means, so it comes once each mean is known.

explain.text: Line 1 writes the wait as a sum, which is the whole trick. Lines 2 and 3 price each piece as a geometric wait. Line 4 is linearity, which needs no independence.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `coupon_expectation(n)`, returning $nH_n$ exactly as a `Fraction`. Then write `coupon_sim(n, trials, seed)`. Each trial draws types $0$ to $n - 1$ with `random.Random(seed)` until all are seen. Return the average number of draws.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.starter:
import random
from fractions import Fraction


def coupon_expectation(n):
    ...


def coupon_sim(n, trials, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 5 need an exact `Fraction`. Tests 6 and 7 accept a simulated mean within three standard errors of $nH_n$. For a die over 20,000 trials that is 0.14. Test 8 runs a seed twice and expects the same answer.

hints.text: Use `Fraction(n, k)` for each stage.
For the simulation, keep a set of types seen and a draw count.
`while len(seen) < n: seen.add(rng.randrange(n)); draws += 1`.

feedback.correct: Exact and simulated answers agree within the noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Return a `Fraction`, not a float: add `Fraction(n, k)` for $k$ from 1 to $n$.
byKey.test-6: The simulated mean is far from 14.7. Check that each trial starts with an empty set and counts every draw.

explain.text: The exact answer is a sum of $n/k$, kept exact by `Fraction`. With seed 1 and 20,000 trials the simulation gives about 14.7, within three standard errors. One trial has a standard deviation of about 6.2 rolls, so the error shrinks like $6.2/\sqrt{\text{trials}}$.

screens.title: A loss on every weekday
screens.prose: A strategy's losing days fall on any of the five weekdays with equal chance, independently of each other. A risk manager wants every weekday to have shown a loss before judging it.

state.caption: Weekdays that have had a losing day so far.

screens.question: How many losing days do you expect before every weekday has had one? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Five equally likely types.
The stage waits are $5/5, 5/4, 5/3, 5/2, 5/1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat weekdays as five coupon types.

byKey.one-each: You allowed one loss per weekday. Repeats on a seen weekday cost extra losing days.
byKey.square: You gave each weekday the last stage's wait of 5.

explain.text: This is the coupon collector with $n = 5$: $5H_5 = 137/12 \approx 11.42$ losing days. Almost half of that, 5 days, is the wait for the last weekday.

ideas: Split a wait for every type into stages, one for each new type.
Stage $k$ is a geometric wait with chance $\tfrac{n - k + 1}{n}$, so it averages $\tfrac{n}{n - k + 1}$ tries.
Linearity adds the stages to $nH_n$, and the last stage alone takes $n$ tries.
summary.trap: Answering about $n$ or $n^2$. The first type takes one try, and the last takes $n$.

quiz.prose: Draw a card from a full deck, note its suit, and put it back. Repeat.
quiz.question: How many draws do you expect until you have seen all four suits? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Four equally likely types: add the four stage waits.

byKey.four: You allowed one draw per suit. Repeats cost extra draws.
byKey.sixteen: You gave every suit the last stage's wait of 4.

explain.text: The waits are $1, \tfrac43, 2, 4$, adding to $\tfrac{25}{3} \approx 8.33$ draws.

quiz.prose: A cereal brand hides one of ten equally likely toys in each box.
quiz.question: How many boxes do you expect to buy to collect all ten? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $10/k$ for $k$ from 1 to 10.

byKey.ten: You allowed one box per toy.
byKey.hundred: You multiplied ten toys by the last wait of ten.

explain.text: $H_{10} \approx 2.929$, so $10H_{10} \approx 29.29$ boxes. The last toy alone takes 10 boxes on average.

quiz.prose: Roll a fair die six times.
quiz.question: How many different faces do you expect to see? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each face, find the chance it appears at least once.

byKey.six: Six rolls rarely show six different faces. Repeats are likely.
byKey.one-minus: That is one face's chance of appearing. Add it over all six faces.

explain.text: Face $j$ appears at least once with chance $1 - (5/6)^6 \approx 0.6651$. Adding over the six faces gives $3.9906$. This counting trick is the next-but-one lesson.

quiz.prose: A collector's set has only one type of card, and every packet holds that card.
quiz.question: How many packets do you expect to open to complete the set?

byKey.zero: You still have to open one packet to hold the card.

explain.text: With $n = 1$ the formula gives $1 \times 1 = 1$: the first packet completes the set. This is the edge case of $nH_n$.
